```{python}
#| echo: false
# Shared setup for every figure in this deck.
import numpy as np
import polars as pl
from plotnine import *

ORANGE = "#f9461c"
DARK = "#c83214"
INK = "#1a1a1a"

def note(x, y, text, ha="left", color=INK, size=13):
    """A text annotation in the deck's type and colors."""
    return annotate("text", x=x, y=y, label=text, ha=ha, size=size, color=color)

def upto(df, col, levels, k, on=0.8):
    """Alpha column: `on` for the first k levels of `col`, 0 for the rest.

    Used with scale_alpha_identity() to render a faceted figure several times
    with the later panels blank. Every panel frame and axis is still computed
    from the full data, so overlaying the versions in an .r-stack fills the
    panels in one at a time without the layout shifting.
    """
    return df.with_columns(
        pl.when(pl.col(col).cast(pl.Utf8).is_in(levels[:k]))
          .then(on).otherwise(0.0).alias("a"))
```

## Random Roll Call {.iframe-slide}
<div class="random-draw" data-num="12" data-min="1" data-max="62">
<div class="random-draw-frame">
<div class="random-draw-numbers" role="status" aria-live="polite" data-placeholder="Press “Draw” for 12 random numbers between 1 and 62."></div>
</div>
<p class="random-draw-controls"><button type="button" class="random-draw-button">Draw</button> <label class="random-draw-sort"><input type="checkbox" class="random-draw-sort-input"> Sort</label> <span class="random-draw-status"></span></p>
</div>

<style>
.random-draw { display: flex; flex-direction: column; flex: 1; min-height: 0; }
.random-draw-frame { flex: 1; min-height: 0; display: flex; justify-content: center; }
.random-draw-numbers { height: 100%; aspect-ratio: 1.618 / 1; max-width: 100%; border: 1px solid #999; display: grid; grid-template-columns: repeat(6, 1fr); grid-template-rows: repeat(2, 1fr); place-items: center; }
.random-draw-numbers .random-draw-number { font-size: 3rem; font-weight: 700; line-height: 1; }
.random-draw-numbers .random-draw-placeholder { grid-column: 1 / -1; grid-row: 1 / -1; text-align: center; font-size: 1.4rem; color: #555; padding: 0 1.5em; }
.random-draw-controls { flex: none; margin: 12px 0 0; }
.random-draw-button { font: inherit; font-size: 1.1rem; font-weight: 600; padding: 0.3em 1.2em; border: none; border-radius: 3px; background: #f9461c; color: #fff; cursor: pointer; }
.random-draw-button:hover:not(:disabled) { background: #e03c14; }
.random-draw-button:disabled { opacity: 0.6; cursor: default; }
.random-draw-sort { font-size: 1rem; color: #555; margin-left: 0.75em; cursor: pointer; }
.random-draw-status { font-size: 1rem; color: #555; margin-left: 0.75em; }
</style>

<script>
(() => {
  // The Sequence Generator, not the Integer Generator: /integers/ samples *with*
  // replacement and silently ignores a `unique` parameter, so a roll call could
  // name the same student twice. /sequences/ returns a shuffled permutation of
  // min..max, and the first `num` of that is a sample without replacement.
  const API = "https://www.random.org/sequences/";
  function setup(root) {
    if (root.dataset.wired) return;
    root.dataset.wired = "1";
    const out = root.querySelector(".random-draw-numbers");
    const button = root.querySelector(".random-draw-button");
    const status = root.querySelector(".random-draw-status");
    const sortBox = root.querySelector(".random-draw-sort-input");
    const num = root.dataset.num, min = root.dataset.min, max = root.dataset.max;
    const url = API + "?min=" + min + "&max=" + max + "&col=1&format=plain&rnd=new";
    let drawn = null;
    function placeholder(text) {
      out.innerHTML = "";
      const p = document.createElement("div");
      p.className = "random-draw-placeholder";
      p.textContent = text;
      out.appendChild(p);
    }
    function render() {
      if (!drawn) return;
      const numbers = sortBox.checked ? drawn.slice().sort(function (a, b) { return a - b; }) : drawn;
      out.innerHTML = "";
      numbers.forEach(function (n) {
        const cell = document.createElement("div");
        cell.className = "random-draw-number";
        cell.textContent = n;
        out.appendChild(cell);
      });
    }
    function draw() {
      button.disabled = true;
      status.textContent = "drawing from random.org…";
      fetch(url, { cache: "no-store" })
        .then(function (r) { if (!r.ok) throw new Error("HTTP " + r.status); return r.text(); })
        .then(function (text) {
          const numbers = text.trim().split(/\s+/).filter(Boolean).map(Number);
          if (!numbers.length) throw new Error("empty response");
          drawn = numbers.slice(0, Number(num));
          render();
          status.textContent = "true random numbers from random.org";
        })
        .catch(function (err) {
          drawn = null;
          placeholder("Could not reach random.org (" + err.message + "). Open the draw in a new tab instead.");
          status.textContent = "";
        })
        .then(function () { button.disabled = false; });
    }
    button.addEventListener("click", draw);
    sortBox.addEventListener("change", render);
    placeholder(out.dataset.placeholder);
  }
  function init() {
    document.querySelectorAll(".random-draw").forEach(setup);
  }
  if (document.readyState === "loading") {
    document.addEventListener("DOMContentLoaded", init);
  } else {
    init();
  }
})();
</script>

::: {.iframe-caption}
Numbers drawn live from <a href="https://www.random.org/sequences/?min=1&max=62&col=1&format=plain&rnd=new">random.org/sequences/?min=1&max=62&col=1&format=plain&rnd=new</a> &mdash; shuffle 1&ndash;62, take first 12.

## The Datasaurus Dozen: Why Visualize? {auto-animate=true}

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="52%"}
::: {.incremental style="font-size:0.72em;"}
- Matejka & Fitzmaurice (CHI 2017) took Alberto Cairo's "Datasaurus" and generated **twelve more datasets** from it.
- Each is nudged point by point toward a target shape, using only moves that leave the summary statistics alone.
- All thirteen have the same mean, standard deviation, and correlation (to two decimals!)
- Summary statistics are a "*lossy compression*"
- Visualization helps
:::
:::
::: {.column width="48%"}

<img data-id="dozen" src="../assets/datasaurus/datasaurus-dozen-panel.svg" class="figure-plain" style="max-height:50vh; margin:0 auto;" alt="All thirteen Datasaurus Dozen datasets as small multiples: dino, star, h_lines, circle, x_shape, v_lines, bullseye, slant_up, dots, slant_down, high_lines, wide_lines, and away">

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis
dino = pl.read_csv("../../datasets/datasaurus-dozen/datasaurus-dozen.csv")
agg = dino.group_by("dataset").agg(
    pl.col("x").mean().alias("mx"), pl.col("y").mean().alias("my"),
    pl.col("x").std().alias("sx"), pl.col("y").std().alias("sy"),
    pl.corr("x", "y").alias("r"))
# U+2212 minus, since a hyphen next to a digit reads as a dash on a slide.
r_bar = f'{agg["r"].mean():.2f}'.replace("-", "−")
print(
    '<div style="text-align:center; font-size:0.55em; color:#565a5c; margin-top:0.3em;">'
    f'across all {agg.height} datasets — '
    f'mean(x) {agg["mx"].mean():.2f}, mean(y) {agg["my"].mean():.2f}, '
    f'sd(x) {agg["sx"].mean():.2f}, sd(y) {agg["sy"].mean():.2f}, '
    f'r {r_bar}</div>'
)
```

# Elements of Visualization {.section-header}

```{python}
#| echo: false
# Setup for the "elements of visualization" slides: one tiny helper for the
# abstract mark demos. The three Chicago map figures (texture, color, value) are
# built ahead of time by datasets/chicago-maps/make_bertin_figures.py and read in
# as SVGs, so this deck no longer loads the geojson.
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt


# Marker paths traced from ../assets/abstraction/0-shapes.svg, so the abstract
# shape demo and the "Shape Anecdote" slide speak the same visual vocabulary.
from matplotlib.path import Path as MplPath

def _poly(points):
    """A closed subpath through `points` (SVG user units, y growing downward)."""
    pts = list(points) + [points[0]]
    codes = [MplPath.MOVETO] + [MplPath.LINETO] * (len(points) - 1) + [MplPath.CLOSEPOLY]
    return pts, codes

def _circle(cx, cy, r, n=64):
    a = np.linspace(0, 2 * np.pi, n, endpoint=False)
    return _poly(list(zip(cx + r * np.cos(a), cy + r * np.sin(a))))

def _rect(x, y, w, h):
    return _poly([(x, y), (x + w, y), (x + w, y + h), (x, y + h)])

def _join(*parts):
    verts, codes = [], []
    for v, c in parts:
        verts += list(v)
        codes += list(c)
    return verts, codes

def _marker(part):
    """Normalize an SVG-space subpath set into a unit-height scatter marker.

    Flipping y and dividing by the bounding-box height means every shape is
    drawn at the same height for a given `s`, so only the form varies.
    """
    verts, codes = part
    v = np.asarray(verts, dtype=float)
    v[:, 1] *= -1
    v /= v[:, 1].max() - v[:, 1].min()
    v -= [(v[:, 0].max() + v[:, 0].min()) / 2, (v[:, 1].max() + v[:, 1].min()) / 2]
    return MplPath(v, codes)

def _teardrop(cx=809.0, cy=488.4, r=104.0, tip=660.0, n=48):
    """Point at the bottom, round over the top -- the upside-down tear.

    Traced curve-for-curve from the SVG: the flanks are cubics that leave the
    tip and meet the semicircle tangentially, so there is no corner where the
    straight sides would otherwise hit the dome.
    """
    a = np.linspace(np.pi, 2 * np.pi, n)  # over the top in SVG's y-down space
    arc = list(zip(cx + r * np.cos(a), cy + r * np.sin(a)))
    verts = ([(cx, tip), (734.12, 576.80), (cx - r, 535.20), (cx - r, cy)]
             + arc[1:]
             + [(cx + r, 535.20), (883.88, 576.80), (cx, tip), (cx, tip)])
    codes = ([MplPath.MOVETO] + [MplPath.CURVE4] * 3
             + [MplPath.LINETO] * (len(arc) - 1)
             + [MplPath.CURVE4] * 3 + [MplPath.CLOSEPOLY])
    return verts, codes

# The Chicago flag's star: six points, one straight up, inner vertices at 0.367 of the
# outer radius -- the flag's own proportion, measured off Chicago-star.png.
STAR = _marker(_poly([
    (219.00, 387.00), (244.05, 480.12), (337.21, 455.25), (269.10, 523.50),
    (337.21, 591.75), (244.05, 566.88), (219.00, 660.00), (193.95, 566.88),
    (100.79, 591.75), (168.90, 523.50), (100.79, 455.25), (193.95, 480.12)]))
SQUARE = _marker(_rect(419.75, 471.50, 188.50, 188.50))
TEARDROP = _marker(_teardrop())
BROCCOLI = _marker(_join(
    _circle(1027.43, 486.71, 80.60), _circle(1104.00, 436.74, 80.60),
    _circle(1180.57, 486.71, 80.60), _rect(1063.70, 486.71, 80.60, 173.29)))
BOLT = _marker(_poly([
    (1419.80, 341.50), (1305.40, 507.12), (1388.60, 507.12), (1336.60, 660.00),
    (1492.60, 468.90), (1403.16, 468.90), (1486.36, 341.50)]))

def mark_axes(ax, xlim=(0, 10), ylim=(0, 6)):
    """A blank frame for the abstract mark demos."""
    ax.set(xlim=xlim, ylim=ylim, xticks=[], yticks=[])
    ax.set_aspect("equal")
    for s in ax.spines.values():
        s.set(color="#c9ccce", linewidth=1)
```

## Position {.text-figure-slide}

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="46%"}
::: {.dense}
- **Position**: the location of a mark within a plane.
- According to Bertin, it is the **base** of the graphic (not a "retinal" variable)
- Scatter plots, bars, maps: position-forward
:::
:::
::: {.column width="54%"}
```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 5.2
#| fig-height: 4.0
#| fig-alt: "Three identical orange dots placed at different spots in an empty frame; nothing about the dots varies except where they are"
fig, ax = plt.subplots()
ax.scatter([1.6, 5.0, 8.4], [1.3, 4.4, 2.6], s=340, color=ORANGE, zorder=3)
mark_axes(ax)
```
:::
:::


---

## Size {.text-figure-slide}

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="46%"}
::: {.dense}
- **Size**: how large or small a mark is (length, area, or volume).
- *Ordered* and *quantitative*: bigger reliably reads as more.
- Also dissociative (small marks are less prominent)
- Can be difficult to compare similar values
:::
:::
::: {.column width="54%"}
```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 5.2
#| fig-height: 4.0
#| fig-alt: "A small orange dot on the left and a much larger orange dot on the right, identical in every way except size"
fig, ax = plt.subplots()
ax.scatter([3.0, 7.0], [3.0, 3.0], s=[120, 2600], color=ORANGE, zorder=3)
mark_axes(ax)
```
:::
:::


---

## Texture (Grain) {.text-figure-slide}

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="46%"}
::: {.dense}
- **Texture** (Bertin's **grain**): how coarse or fine a fill pattern is.
- only the scale changes changes in this example
- Land is coarse, water is fine
- Categorical (not *quantitative*)
:::
:::
::: {.column width="54%"}
![](../assets/bertin-maps/bertin-texture.svg){.figure alt="Map of Chicago drawn only in black and white: the land is filled with a coarse dot pattern and Lake Michigan and the rivers with a much finer dot pattern"}
:::
:::


---

## Color (Hue) {.text-figure-slide}

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="46%"}
::: {.dense}
::: {}
- **Color** for Bertin means only **hue** (lightness is fixed)
- Example: same map, same two areas, only hue is different.
- **Not ordered.** (Blue is not "more" than tan)
- So hue/color encodes identity/category (not magnitude)
:::
:::
:::
::: {.column width="54%"}
![](../assets/bertin-maps/bertin-color.svg){.figure alt="The same map of Chicago, now with land filled in sand and Lake Michigan and the rivers filled in teal"}
:::
:::


---

## Value {.text-figure-slide}

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="46%"}
::: {.dense}
- **Value**: lightness (independent of hue)
- "Hue" is grey in this example, "value" is how dark
- Chicago's 50 wards, shaded by median household income
- *ordered*: darker reads as "more."
- **dissociative** (like size), i.e. affects prominence / hierarchy
- Two different greys can be visually "ranked" (but that's about it)
:::
:::
::: {.column width="54%"}
![](../assets/bertin-maps/bertin-value.svg){.figure alt="Choropleth map of Chicago's 50 wards shaded from pale grey to near-black by estimated median household income, with the darkest wards along the north lakefront"}
:::
:::



---

## Orientation {.text-figure-slide}

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="46%"}
::: {.dense}
- **Orientation**: the angle a mark is tilted.
- Identical bars; only the angle varies.
- *Selective* and *associative*: easy to see, adds no "ink"
- Not necessarily ordered, for points and lines : 30° is not "more" than 60°.
- Can conflict with texture.
:::
:::
::: {.column width="54%"}
```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 5.2
#| fig-height: 4.0
#| fig-alt: "Five identical orange bars in a row, each tilted to a different angle from horizontal through vertical"
fig, ax = plt.subplots()
for x, deg in zip([1.4, 3.2, 5.0, 6.8, 8.6], [0, 30, 60, 90, 135]):
    t = np.deg2rad(deg)
    dx, dy = 1.05 * np.cos(t), 1.05 * np.sin(t)
    ax.plot([x - dx, x + dx], [3 - dy, 3 + dy], color=ORANGE, lw=7,
            solid_capstyle="round")
mark_axes(ax)
```
:::
:::


---

## Shape {.text-figure-slide}

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="46%"}
::: {.dense}
::: {}
- **Shape**: the form of the mark, at constant size and "ink"
- Weakest variable according to Bertin
- The eye cannot easily collect "all the triangles"
    - searches one at a time.
- Not ordered, not quantitative, just labels categories.
:::
:::
:::
::: {.column width="54%"}
```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 5.2
#| fig-height: 4.0
#| fig-alt: "Five orange marks in a row at the same height: a six-pointed Chicago-flag star, a square, an upside-down teardrop, a broccoli floret and a lightning bolt"
fig, ax = plt.subplots()
for x, m in zip([1.4, 3.2, 5.0, 6.8, 8.6], [STAR, SQUARE, TEARDROP, BROCCOLI, BOLT]):
    ax.scatter([x], [3], marker=m, s=1600, color=ORANGE, zorder=3)
mark_axes(ax)
```
:::
:::

## All Seven Variables{.image-frame-slide}

<img src="../assets/bertins-visual-variables/bertins-visual-variables.svg" alt="Table of Bertin's seven visual variables. Each row pairs a name and definition with a demonstration: position shows one mark at four locations; size shows length, area and repetition; shape shows eight silhouettes; value shows a ten-step ramp from white to black; colour shows ten hues at one lightness; orientation shows one stripe pattern at four angles; texture shows the same pattern at four grains.">

## Munzner's Channels {.smaller}

From Tamara Munzner's *Visualization Analysis & Design* (2014), which uses the term **channels**. Ranking is based on the Cleveland & McGill graphical-perception experiments.
 :

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {style="font-size:0.82em;"}
**Magnitude channels** : ordered attributes, most to least effective:

1. Position on a common scale
2. Position on an unaligned scale
3. Length (1D size)
4. Tilt / angle
5. Area (2D size)
6. Depth (3D position)
7. Color luminance / saturation
8. Curvature
9. Volume (3D size)
:::
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {style="font-size:0.82em;"}
**Identity channels** : categorical attributes:

1. Spatial region
2. Color hue
3. **Motion**
4. Shape
:::

:::
:::

# Distributions of One Variable {.section-header}

---

##  Kinds of Visualization

::: {}
- **Exploratory Data Visualization:** figuring out what is true. Mostly for you and/or your team.
- **Persuasive Data Visualization:** convincing other people something is true. Polished, for an audience.
:::

::: {style="margin-top:1em;"}
We will start with exploratory/descriptive visualization, then move to persuasive visualization ("visualization rhetoric")
:::

---

## Choosing a Plot: Quantitative Data

**Plots:** histograms, box plots, rug plots, smoothed interpolations (KDE : kernel density estimators)

::: {}
- **Histogram** : relative frequency of values; there's a tradeoff in choosing bin sizes.
- **Rug plot** : shows where the actual data points sit.
- **KDE plot** : a smoothed density estimate; there's a tradeoff in the "bandwidth" parameter.
:::

::: {style="margin-top:0.8em;"}
**Look for:** spread, shape, modes, gaps, outliers, unreasonable values.
:::

---

## Some Made-Up Data

```{python}
#| echo: true
rng = np.random.default_rng(418)
d = np.concatenate([rng.normal(5, 3, 45), rng.normal(30, 6, 170),
                    rng.normal(80, 3, 7)])
dist = pl.DataFrame({"v": d})
```

::: {style="font-size:0.8em; margin-top:0.4em;"}
Three groups together: a small one near 5, a big one near 30, and seven near 80.
:::

## Histogram {.code-figure-slide}

```{python}
#| echo: true
#| fig-alt: "Histogram of the made-up data with 32 bins, showing a small mode near 5, a large mode near 30, and a few isolated bars near 80"
(ggplot(dist, aes("v"))
 + geom_histogram(bins=32, fill=ORANGE, alpha=0.85,
                  color="white", size=0.3)
 + labs(x="Value", y="Count")
 + theme_minimal(base_size=14))
```

::: {style="font-size:0.8em;"}
Counts values falling in each bin (`bins` is the main knob to adjust)
:::

## Too Few Bins {.code-figure-slide}

```{python}
#| echo: true
#| fig-alt: "Histogram of the same data with only 4 bins, collapsing the two groups into one tall bar and hiding the gap before the outliers"
(ggplot(dist, aes("v"))
 + geom_histogram(bins=4, fill=ORANGE, alpha=0.85,
                  color="white", size=0.3)
 + labs(x="Value", y="Count")
 + theme_minimal(base_size=14))
```

::: {style="font-size:0.8em;"}
**Oversmoothed.** The two groups merge into one bar, and the gap before the outliers disappears. The shape looks simpler than the data actually is.
:::

---

## Too Many Bins {.code-figure-slide}

```{python}
#| echo: true
#| fig-alt: "Histogram of the same data with 300 bins, producing a spiky comb of mostly one- and two-count bars where the overall shape is hard to see"
(ggplot(dist, aes("v"))
 + geom_histogram(bins=300, fill=ORANGE, alpha=0.85,
                  color="white", size=0.3)
 + labs(x="Value", y="Count")
 + theme_minimal(base_size=14))
```

::: {style="font-size:0.8em;"}
**Undersmoothed.** Most bins hold one or two points, so the bars mostly report sampling noise.
:::

---

## Rug Plot {.code-figure-slide}

```{python}
#| echo: true
#| fig-alt: "Rug plot of the made-up data: a dense band of tick marks near 30, a sparser band near 5, an empty stretch, and a handful of ticks near 80"
(ggplot(dist, aes("v", 0))
 + geom_rug(sides="b", color=INK, alpha=0.4, length=0.5)
 + labs(x="Value")
 + theme_minimal(base_size=14)
 + theme(panel_grid=element_blank(),
         axis_title_y=element_blank(),
         axis_text_y=element_blank()))
```

::: {style="font-size:0.8em;"}
One tick per data point (no binning, no smoothing). Great for spotting gaps and outliers; less helpful once the ticks overlap into a solid block.
:::

---

## KDE Plot {.code-figure-slide}

```{python}
#| echo: true
#| fig-alt: "Two kernel density curves over the same data: a smooth solid curve with two clear modes, and a wigglier dashed curve from a smaller bandwidth"
(ggplot(dist, aes("v"))
 + geom_density(size=1.2)                   # default bandwidth
 + geom_density(alpha=0.6, size=1.0, linetype="dashed",
                adjust=0.25)                              # 1/4 the bandwidth
 + labs(x="Value", y="Density")
 + theme_minimal(base_size=14))
```

::: {style="font-size:0.8em;"}
A smoothed estimate of the density. **`adjust` scales the bandwidth:** the dashed curve is noisy, the solid one may smooth over real structure.
:::

---

## All Three at Once {.figure-slide}

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 4.2
#| fig-alt: "A histogram of a bimodal distribution with a kernel density curve drawn over it and a rug of individual points along the bottom axis, annotated to point out the main mode, a second mode, a right skew, a gap, and a cluster of outliers"
(ggplot(dist, aes("v"))
 + geom_histogram(aes(y=after_stat("density")), bins=32,
                  fill=ORANGE, alpha=0.35, color="white", size=0.3)
 + geom_density(color=DARK, size=1.2)
 + geom_rug(color=INK, alpha=0.4, length=0.04)
 + note(44, 0.052, "Main mode")
 + note(-6, 0.030, "Second mode")
 + note(46, 0.014, "Skew right")
 + note(56, 0.004, "Gap")
 + note(70, 0.012, "Outliers", color=DARK)
 + note(14, 0.040, "KDE", color=DARK)
 + note(-6, 0.006, "Rug")
 + labs(y="Density")
 + theme_minimal(base_size=14)
 + theme(axis_title_x=element_blank(), figure_size=(10, 4.2)))
```

---

## Choosing a Plot: Categorical Data
**Plots:** bar plots, sorted by frequency or by the ordinal dimension

::: {}
- **Look for:** skew, frequent and rare categories, invalid categories.
- For **ordinal** data (e.g. education level: < 12th, HS, Trade, Some College, College), keep the relevant order.
- **Dot plots** (Cleveland dot plots) make it easier to compare
:::


---

## Bar Plot (for an Ordinal Variable) {.figure-slide}

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 4.2
#| fig-alt: "Bar chart of mothers' education level with five bars in their natural order from less than 12th grade through college; high school is the tallest bar and trade school the shortest"
levels = ["< 12th", "HS", "Trade", "Some college", "College"]
edu = pl.DataFrame({
    "level": levels,
    "count": [201, 449, 61, 297, 219],
}).with_columns(pl.col("level").cast(pl.Enum(levels)))

(ggplot(edu, aes("level", "count"))
 + geom_col(fill=ORANGE, alpha=0.85, width=0.6)
 + labs(x="Education level", y="Count")
 + theme_minimal(base_size=15)
 + theme(figure_size=(10, 4.2)))
```

::: {style="font-size:0.6em; margin-top:0.2em;"}
The bars keep the natural order of the levels, not shortest-to-tallest.
:::

---

## "Lollipop" Chart of the Same Data {.figure-slide}

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 4.2
#| fig-alt: "Lollipop chart of the same five education-level counts, with one dot per level at the end of an orange stem running out from the axis, which can make the values easier to compare than the bars"
(ggplot(edu, aes("count", "level"))
 + geom_segment(aes(x=0, xend="count", y="level", yend="level"),
                color=ORANGE, size=1.5, alpha=0.85)
 + geom_point(color=ORANGE, size=5)
 + labs(x="Count", y="Education level")
 + theme_minimal(base_size=15)
 + theme(figure_size=(10, 4.2)))
```

::: {style="font-size:0.6em; margin-top:0.2em;"}
Same numbers as the bars, less "ink."
:::

---

## Line Graphs and Time Series {.figure-aside}

::: {.aside-note}
*Computational and Inferential Thinking*, [Chapter 7: Visualization](https://inferentialthinking.com/chapters/07/visualization)
:::

::: {.columns}
::: {.column}
- A **line graph** connects points in the order of the x variable : usually time.
- A line between two points implies order
- When categories are on the x-axis, avoid lines.
- *More on time series soon.*
:::
::: {.column}

<img class="figure" src="../assets/viz-basics/time-series-line.svg" alt="Two panels of the same CTA annual rail boardings, 1999 to 2025. On the left the years are drawn as separate dots; on the right the same dots are connected, and the steady climb to 2015, the 2020 collapse and the partial recovery all become visible as one shape.">
:::
:::


---

## Reading a Histogram by Area {.figure-aside .smaller}

::: {.aside-note}
*Computational and Inferential Thinking*, [Section 7.2: Visualizing Numerical Distributions](https://inferentialthinking.com/chapters/07/2/visualizing-numerical-distributions)
:::

::: {.columns}
::: {.column}
- In a bar chart, **height** is the value. In a histogram, **area** is the value.
- The **area principle**: a two-dimensional figure should encode the magnitude in its *area*, not just its height.
- So the height is $\dfrac{\text{percent in bin}}{\text{bin width}}$ : a **density**
- All the areas sum to 100%.
- Bins do not have to be equal width. If they are not, only the density scale is readable.
:::
::: {.column}

<img class="figure" src="../assets/viz-basics/histogram-area.svg" alt="Two panels of the same Cook County sale prices in five uneven bins: four $100k bins and one $500k bin. On the density scale the wide bin is one of the shortest bars even though 35 percent of sales fall in it; plotted as raw counts the same bin is by far the tallest.">

::: {.caption}
The widest bin holds the most sales (35%) and is nearly the *shortest* bar : it is the least crowded.
:::
:::
:::


---

## Vocabulary for Describing Common Shapes
Many models assume features are **symmetric** and **unimodal**. Deviations can affect the validity of the model.

::: {}
- **Symmetric** : looks the same on the left and right sides.
- **Skewed** : one tail is longer than the other (right or left).
- **Unimodal** : a single mode (peak).
- **Multimodal** : multiple modes (peaks).
:::


---

## Three Shapes {.figure-slide}

```{python}
#| echo: false
rng = np.random.default_rng(1848)
shapes = ["Symmetric, unimodal", "Right-skewed", "Multimodal"]
shape_df = pl.DataFrame({
    "v": np.concatenate([
        rng.normal(0, 1, 600),
        rng.exponential(1, 600),
        np.concatenate([rng.normal(-2, 0.6, 300), rng.normal(2, 0.6, 300)]),
    ]),
    "shape": np.repeat(shapes, 600),
}).with_columns(pl.col("shape").cast(pl.Enum(shapes)))

def shape_plot(k):
    return (ggplot(upto(shape_df, "shape", shapes, k), aes("v"))
     + geom_histogram(aes(alpha="a"), bins=28, fill=ORANGE,
                      color="white", size=0.3)
     + scale_alpha_identity()
     + facet_wrap("shape", scales="free_x")
     + labs(y="Count")
     + theme_minimal(base_size=15)
     + theme(axis_title_x=element_blank(),
             strip_text=element_text(size=16, color=INK),
             panel_spacing=0.06, figure_size=(10, 4)))
```

::: {.r-stack}

::: {.fragment .fade-out fragment-index=1}
```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 4
#| fig-alt: "Three histogram panels side by side; only the first is filled in, showing a symmetric unimodal bell shape"
shape_plot(1)
```
:::

::: {.fragment .fade-in-then-out fragment-index=1}
```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 4
#| fig-alt: "The same three panels with the first two filled in: a symmetric bell shape and a right-skewed distribution with a long tail to the right"
shape_plot(2)
```
:::

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 4
#| fig-alt: "All three panels filled in: a symmetric unimodal bell shape, a right-skewed distribution with a long tail to the right, and a multimodal distribution with two separated peaks"
shape_plot(3)
```

# Relationships Between Variables {.section-header}

---

## Identifying Relationships
::: {}
- Features in a dataset are usually related to each other. **Linear** relationships are the simplest type.
- **Correlation** describes the *strength* and *direction* of a linear relationship between two features.
  - **Positive** correlation : one feature increases as the other increases.
  - **Negative** correlation : one feature decreases as the other increases.
- We explore relationships using **scatter plots**: positive correlation, negative correlation, or no linear correlation.
:::

---

## Three Scatter Plots {.figure-slide}

```{python}
#| echo: false
rng = np.random.default_rng(418)
x = rng.uniform(0, 10, 90)
kinds = ["Positive correlation", "Negative correlation", "No linear correlation"]
corr_df = pl.DataFrame({
    "x": np.tile(x, 3),
    "y": np.concatenate([x + rng.normal(0, 1.5, 90),
                         -x + rng.normal(0, 1.5, 90),
                         rng.uniform(0, 10, 90)]),
    "kind": np.repeat(kinds, 90),
}).with_columns(pl.col("kind").cast(pl.Enum(kinds)))

def corr_plot(k):
    return (ggplot(upto(corr_df, "kind", kinds, k, on=0.75), aes("x", "y"))
     + geom_point(aes(alpha="a"), color=ORANGE, size=2.5)
     + scale_alpha_identity()
     + facet_wrap("kind", scales="free_y")
     + theme_minimal(base_size=15)
     + theme(axis_title=element_blank(), axis_text=element_blank(),
             strip_text=element_text(size=16, weight="bold", color=INK),
             panel_spacing=0.06, figure_size=(10, 4)))
```

::: {.r-stack}

::: {.fragment .fade-out fragment-index=1}
```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 4
#| fig-alt: "Three scatter plot panels side by side; only the first has points, trending upward for positive correlation"
corr_plot(1)
```
:::

::: {.fragment .fade-in-then-out fragment-index=1}
```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 4
#| fig-alt: "The same three panels with the first two filled in: points trending upward, then points trending downward for negative correlation"
corr_plot(2)
```
:::

::: {.fragment fragment-index=2}
```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 4
#| fig-alt: "All three panels filled in: points trending upward (positive correlation), points trending downward (negative correlation), and points with no visible trend (no linear correlation)"
corr_plot(3)
```
:::

:::

---

## Correlation Coefficient

The correlation coefficient measures the linear relationship between two features $X$ and $Y$. We'll use **Pearson's correlation coefficient** first.

::: {}
- The value is always between **-1 and 1**.
- The sign gives the direction
- The closer to -1 or 1, the stronger the relationship.
- A coefficient of **0** means there is no *linear* relationship
    - not the same as no relationship
:::

---

## Setup: Chicago 'L' ridership, 2019

Are stations that are busy on weekdays also busy on Saturdays?

```{python}
#| echo: true
cta = pl.read_csv("../../datasets/cta-ridership/Station_Entries_-_Daily_Totals_20260527.csv",
                  ignore_errors=True)
cta = cta.with_columns(pl.col("rides").str.replace_all(",", "").cast(pl.Int64))
by_day = (cta.filter(pl.col("date").str.ends_with("2019"))
             .group_by("stationname", "daytype")
             .agg(pl.col("rides").median()))
stations = by_day.pivot("daytype", index="stationname", values="rides")
```

::: {style="font-size:0.8em; margin-top:0.4em;"}
`daytype` is `W` for weekdays, `A` for Saturdays, `U` for Sundays and holidays.
:::

---

## Weekday vs. Saturday {.code-figure-slide}

```{python}
#| echo: true
#| fig-alt: "Scatter plot of 144 Chicago 'L' stations, median weekday entries on the x-axis against median Saturday entries on the y-axis, showing a strong upward linear trend"
(ggplot(stations, aes("W", "A"))
 + geom_point(alpha=0.7)
 + labs(x="Median weekday entries", y="Median Saturday entries")
 + theme_minimal())
```

---

## How strong is it? (CTA Ridership)

```{python}
#| echo: true
# W = median weekday entries, A = median Saturday entries
stations.select(pl.corr("W", "A")).item()
```

::: {style="font-size:0.85em; margin-top:0.8em;"}
Strong and positive: busy stations are busy on both days. Not *perfect* : Loop stations serving commuters drop off far more on a Saturday than neighborhood stations do.
:::

---

## Setup: Cook County home sales, 2025

Do bigger houses sell for more money?

```{python}
#| echo: true
sales = pl.read_csv("../../datasets/cook-county-home-sales-2025/cook-county-home-sales-2025.csv",
                    ignore_errors=True)
homes = sales.filter(
    (pl.col("property_group") == "Single-Family")   # condos have no sqft
    & (pl.col("is_multisale") == False)             # one price per home
    & (pl.col("sale_price") > 10_000)               # drop nominal transfers
    & pl.col("building_sqft").is_not_null()
)
homes.height
```

---

## The Cone Shape
::: {}
- The points **fan out** as houses get larger
    - Small homes cluster in a price band, large homes all over
- A single correlation coefficient reports one number for the whole cloud,
- can hide a stronger relationship at one end versus the other.
- Always look at the scatter plot.
- **The coefficient is only a summary.**
:::


---

## Correlation Pitfalls: The Simpson's Paradox {.image-frame-slide}

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
<img class="figure" src="../assets/viz-basics/simpsons-paradox-pooled.svg" alt="Scatter plot of salary against years of seniority for 960 employees drawn as one grey cloud, with a fitted line falling from about $230k at half a year to about $100k at seven years.">
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
<img class="figure fragment" src="../assets/viz-basics/simpsons-paradox-split.svg" alt="The same 960 points colored by department. Data science sits high and junior, product in the middle, HR low and senior, and the fitted line within each department rises with seniority.">
:::
:::

::: {.caption .fragment}
Synthetic data. Pooled, salary **falls** with seniority; within every department it **rises**.
:::

---

## Simpson's Paradox in the Wild: Batting Averages {.smaller}

::: {.aside-note}
Ken Ross, *A Mathematician at the Ballpark* : Derek Jeter and David Justice, 1995 and 1996.
:::

::: {.batting}
|                  | 1995 | 1996 | Combined |
|------------------|:---:|:---:|:---:|
| **Derek Jeter**  | 12/48 = .250 | 183/582 = .314 | 195/630 = **.310** |
| **David Justice**| 104/411 = **.253** | 45/140 = **.321** | 149/551 = .270 |
:::

<style>
/* Four columns of the same width, so the two name cells stop eating the row
   and no at-bats line has to wrap mid-fraction. */
.batting td, .batting th { white-space: nowrap; }
.batting td:first-child, .batting th:first-child { width: 25%; }
.batting td:not(:first-child), .batting th:not(:first-child) { width: 25%; }
</style>

::: {.fragment}
- Justice hit for a higher average in **each** season and a lower average **combined**
- Check the at-bats:
    - Jeter's better year is his "heavy" year
    - Justice's better year is his "light" year
:::

---

## Visualizing Bivariate Relationships

::: {}
- A **scatter plot** helps uncover the *form* of the relationship between two quantitative variables.
- **Linear** relationships are the simplest to interpret : and there is a lot of clean statistical theory for them.
- Models are approximations. Prefer the simpler one until the data forces you to a more complex one.
:::

## Visualizing Uncertainty {.figure-aside}

::: {.aside-note}
*Fundamentals of Data Visualization*, [Chapter 16: Visualizing Uncertainty](https://clauswilke.com/dataviz/visualizing-uncertainty.html)
:::

- Almost every number in a plot is an **estimate**
- **Error bars** (or a band) show how the estimate could move.
- *More details soon.*

<img class="figure figure-sm" src="../assets/viz-basics/uncertainty-intervals.svg" alt="Two panels of the same four mean sale prices by bedroom count. On the left, plain grey bars. On the right, the same means as dots with 95 percent interval whiskers, and the 4- and 5-plus-bedroom intervals overlap substantially.">

::: {.caption}
The 4- and 5+ intervals overlap: on this sample those two means are not distinguishable.
:::


# Perception: Color & Length {.section-header}

---

## Color Blindness {.text-figure-slide}

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="38%"}
::: {.dense}
::: {}
- Picking colors that work together can be difficult
- **7–10% of men** have red-green color vision deficiency (deuteranomaly is the common one).
- Blue-yellow deficiency is far less common.
- Red and green is the worst pair (try to avoid)
:::
:::
:::
::: {.column width="62%"}
<img class="figure" src="../assets/viz-basics/color-red-green.svg" alt="Two line charts side by side. On the left, three series of median 2025 sale price by bedroom count drawn in red, green and brown. On the right, the same chart run through a deuteranope simulation, where the red and green lines have collapsed into nearly the same olive colour.">

::: {.caption}
Simulation uses Viénot, Brettel & Mollon (1999).
:::
:::
:::

---

## Redundant Encoding {.image-frame-slide}

<img src="../assets/viz-basics/color-redundant.svg" alt="The same three-series chart drawn in Okabe-Ito blue, vermillion and green with solid, dashed and dotted line styles, beside its deuteranope simulation. The three series remain distinguishable in both panels because the dash pattern carries the identity as well as the hue.">

::: {style="font-size:0.8em; margin-top:0.4em;"}
In general, try to avoid hue being the only channel (add dash, shape, and/or direct label)
:::

---

## Colorfulness {.image-frame-slide}

<img src="../assets/viz-basics/color-saturation.svg" alt="The same chart twice: on the left in fully saturated pure red, green and blue, on the right in muted orange, steel grey and dusty blue. The muted version is markedly easier to look at.">


---

## Perceptually Uniform Colormaps {.image-frame-slide}

::: {.caption}
Design story: Nathaniel Smith and Stéfan van der Walt, "A Better Default Colormap for Matplotlib" (SciPy 2015), <https://bids.github.io/colormap>.
:::

<img src="../assets/viz-basics/colormap-luminance.svg" alt="Two colormap strips, jet and viridis, above a plot of their perceived lightness. Viridis climbs in a straight line from dark to light; jet zig-zags up and back down, with a bright band in the middle and dark at both ends.">

::: {style="font-size:0.8em; margin-top:0.4em;"}
A colormap should have **uniform perceptual deltas**: equal steps in the data should look like equal steps. `jet` does not
:::



---

## Data Type and Color {.text-figure-slide}

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="42%"}
::: {.dense}
::: {}
- **Categorical** : pick a scheme that makes categories easy to *tell apart*.
    - No order implied.
- **Quantitative, low→high** : use **sequential** schemes; light for low.
- **Quantitative, two meaningful ends** : use a **diverging** scheme; light in the middle.
- Getting this wrong can be a real mistake (not just aesthetic / subjective)
:::
:::
:::
::: {.column width="58%"}
<img class="figure" src="../assets/viz-basics/color-schemes.svg" alt="Three rows of eight colour swatches: a categorical row of maximally distinct Okabe-Ito hues, a sequential row running from pale cream to dark brown, and a diverging row running dark blue through near-white to dark red.">

::: {.caption}
Categorical row is the Okabe & Ito palette, ["Color Universal Design"](https://jfly.uni-koeln.de/color/) (2008).
:::
:::
:::

---

## Length Versus Area {.image-frame-slide}

<img src="../assets/viz-basics/area-vs-length.svg" alt="Left: eight circles, one per CTA 'L' line, sized so that circle area encodes median weekday entries; the Red Line circle is the largest and the Yellow Line circle is a dot. Right: the same eight values as a dot plot on a common scale, where the Red Line's 180 thousand entries is plainly about three times the Orange Line's 59 thousand.">

# Pie & Donut Charts {.section-header}


## Pie Charts Intuition

- A pie chart encodes **proportion** as **angle** (and area)
- Works okay for simple comparisons, single data points
- E.g. "roughly half" or "roughly a quarter"
- Difficult to compare multiple slices

---

## The Principle of Proportional Ink {.figure-aside}

::: {.aside-note}
Bergstrom & West, *Calling Bullshit*, [7.3: The Principle of Proportional Ink](https://www.callingbullshit.org/tools/tools_proportional_ink.html)
:::

::: {.columns}
::: {.column}
- **The "ink" used should be directly proportional to the quantity shown.**
- A bar is a length *from zero*
- Same rule applies to Steve Jobs' 3D pie chart
- Lines and dots encode **position**
    - can start wherever the data starts
:::
::: {.column}

<img class="figure" src="../assets/viz-basics/proportional-ink.svg" alt="Two bar charts of the same five CTA annual rail boarding totals, 2015 to 2019. Drawn from zero the bars are nearly equal and drift gently down; drawn from 210 million the 2019 bar is a small fraction of the 2015 bar and the decline looks like a collapse.">

::: {.caption}
Ridership fell, but the panels tell different stories.
:::
:::
:::

---

## Never Do a 3D Pie Chart

::: {}
- Never ever ever ever ever ever ever do a 3D pie chart
- Why?
    - Perspective distorts angle and area
    - Slices in the front (near the viewer) look larger
    - The tilt changes how big a slice appears (independent of data)
    - adds a dimension that carries no information
:::

## The Donut Chart {.figure-aside}

::: {.columns}
::: {.column}
- A **donut chart** is a pie chart with the center cut out
- Keeps the "this is all part of a whole" message
- Slices are still difficult to compare
- Here are Steve Jobs' numbers again, as a donut

## Concluding Notes: Visual EDA

::: {}
**One-dimensional data**

- Summarize with summary statistics (`df.describe()`)
- Visualize the distribution with histograms and box plots.
:::

::: {}
**Two-dimensional data**

- Visualize the relationship with scatter plots.
- Measure relationships with correlations.
:::

::: {}
**High-dimensional data**

- Create a **scatterplot matrix** (all pairwise scatter plots)
- Create a **correlation matrix** (all pairwise correlations)
:::

::: {}
**Correlations can mislead**

- Additional variables may reveal unexpected and contrasting results.
:::

## Seven Things to Watch

::: {}
1. **Scale** : what are the axes, and do they start where they should?
2. **Conditioning** : what did you hold fixed to make the comparison?
3. **Context** : units, reference values, labels, a caption.
4. **Transformations** : logs and their friends.
5. **Perception: color** : hue is a weak channel and not everyone sees it the same.
6. **Perception: length** : length beats angle, area, and volume.
7. **Causality** and **large N** : two ways a correct plot still misleads.
:::

# Scale, Conditioning & Context {.section-header}

---

## 2015 Congressional Hearing: Planned Parenthood

::: {}
- Rep. Jason Chaffetz (R-UT), then chair of the House Oversight Committee, was questioning federal funding of Planned Parenthood.
- He displayed a chart that had first appeared in a report by Americans United for Life.
- The chart plots two services : cancer screenings and abortions : from 2006 to 2013.
:::




---

## The Chart as Shown {.image-frame-slide}

<img src="../assets/viz-basics/scale-two-axes.svg" alt="Two thick lines crossing. A pale line labelled Cancer screening falls from 2,007,371 in 2006 to 935,573 in 2013; an orange line labelled Abortion rises from 289,750 to 327,000. There is no y-axis and no gridline.">

::: {.caption}
Redrawn from the chart displayed at the House Oversight Committee hearing, 29 September 2015 (originally from an Americans United for Life report).
:::

---

## What is suspicious about this plot? {.split .smaller}

::: {.split-content .golden-columns}

::: {}

<img class="figure" src="../assets/viz-basics/scale-two-axes.svg" alt="Two thick lines crossing. A pale line labelled Cancer screening falls from 2,007,371 in 2006 to 935,573 in 2013; an orange line labelled Abortion rises from 289,750 to 327,000. There is no y-axis and no gridline." style="max-height:320px; margin-bottom:0.5em;">

1. **How many data points** are actually in this plot?
2. What is the **y-axis**?
3. Why do the two lines cross?
4. How would you fix it?
:::

<iframe src="https://dodatascience.fun/timer/" title="CTA-style countdown timer" loading="lazy" style="width: 100%; height: 420px; display: block; border: 1px solid #999; box-shadow: 0 10px 28px rgba(0,0,0,0.12); border-radius: 3px;"></iframe>

:::

---

## The Same Four Numbers, One Scale {.image-frame-slide}

<img src="../assets/viz-basics/scale-one-axis.svg" alt="The same two series on one shared y-axis running from zero to 2.2 million services. Cancer screening falls steeply from just over 2 million to under 1 million; the abortion line is nearly flat near 300,000 and the two never come close to crossing.">

::: {style="font-size:0.8em; margin-top:0.4em;"}
Now the dominant fact is visible: cancer screenings **fell by half**, and abortions barely moved. Nothing crosses.
:::

---

## Or Plot the Quantity in Dispute {.image-frame-slide}

<img src="../assets/viz-basics/scale-percent.svg" alt="Bar chart with two bars. Abortions as a share of the two services rise from 13 percent in 2006 to 26 percent in 2013.">

::: {style="font-size:0.8em; margin-top:0.4em;"}
The argument was about **mix**, not counts. As a share, abortions went from 13% to 26% : which the original chart never actually showed, even though it was trying to.
:::

---

## Conditioning

**Conditioning** means holding one variable fixed : or slicing by it : so that a comparison means something.

::: {}
- Split into groups and draw side-by-side bars, boxes, or panels.
- Bin a continuous variable (ages in decades, homes by bedroom count) and compare within bins.
- The Bertin/Munzner language for this is a **small multiple**: same encoding, repeated.
:::

::: {style="margin-top:0.6em;"}
Every conditioning choice is a claim about what else was going on. Say it out loud.
:::

---

## Grouped Bars {.image-frame-slide}

<img src="../assets/viz-basics/conditioning-bars.svg" alt="Grouped bar chart of median 2025 sale price by bedroom count, with a Chicago bar and a suburban Cook County bar in each group. Both rise steeply from 2 to 5-plus bedrooms.">

::: {style="font-size:0.8em; margin-top:0.4em;"}
Median sale price, conditioned on bedroom count and on Chicago vs. suburban Cook County.
:::

---

## Which comparisons are easy here? {.split .smaller}

::: {.split-content .golden-columns}

::: {}

<img class="figure" src="../assets/viz-basics/conditioning-bars.svg" alt="Grouped bar chart of median 2025 sale price by bedroom count, with a Chicago bar and a suburban Cook County bar in each group. Both rise steeply from 2 to 5-plus bedrooms." style="max-height:320px; margin-bottom:0.5em;">

1. Which comparisons can you make **easily**?
2. Which comparison is most **interesting** or important?
3. Are those the same comparison?
:::

## Same Numbers, Less Ink {.image-frame-slide}

::: {.r-stack}
<div class="fragment fade-out" data-fragment-index="1"><img src="../assets/viz-basics/conditioning-dots.svg" alt="Cleveland dot plot of the same medians: one row per bedroom count, with a Chicago dot and a suburban dot joined by a thin connector. The connectors get longer as bedrooms increase."></div>

<div class="fragment" data-fragment-index="1"><img src="../assets/viz-basics/conditioning-lines.svg" alt="The same medians as two connected lines with the space between them lightly shaded, annotated with a 90 thousand dollar gap at 5-plus bedrooms."></div>

Dots put both values on a common scale. Lines make the **gap** itself the shape of the chart : which is the comparison we actually wanted.
:::

## What is missing? {.split .smaller}

::: {.split-content .golden-columns}

::: {}

<img class="figure" src="../assets/viz-basics/context-bare.svg" alt="A single orange line rising gradually, then falling off a cliff near the right edge and partly recovering. The axes have bare numbers and no labels, titles, or units." style="max-height:300px; margin-bottom:0.5em;">

:::

---

## The Same Line, With Context {.text-figure-slide}

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="40%"}
::: {.dense}
::: {}
- Label the axes, and **include units**.
- Add **reference lines** for values that matter.
- Label the unusual or interesting **points**.
- Write a **caption**: what the data is, how it is plotted, what to look at.
:::
:::
:::
::: {.column width="60%"}
<img class="figure" src="../assets/viz-basics/context-annotated.svg" alt="The same CTA rail boardings line, now titled, with a y-axis labelled in millions, a dashed reference line at the 1999 level, a marked 2015 peak of 242 million rides, an annotation on the 2020 pandemic collapse, and a source line.">
:::
:::

# Transformations {.section-header}

---

## Why Transform a Variable?

::: {}
- To **reveal the distribution of most of the observations** : otherwise the bulk of the data is squashed into a corner.
- To **reveal anomalies** on the far side of a long tail.
- To turn a **curved** relationship into a straight one you can reason about.
:::

::: {style="margin-top:0.8em;"}
**Logarithmic transformations take care of most needs.**
:::

---

## Standardize or Normalize? {.text-figure-slide}

::: {.aside-note}
*Computational and Inferential Thinking*, [Section 14.2: Standard Units](https://inferentialthinking.com/chapters/14/2/variability/#standard-units)
:::

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="38%"}
::: {.incremental style="font-size:0.82em; padding-right:24px;"}
- **Standardize** (z-score): $(x - \bar{x})/s$: center 0, spread 1.
- **Normalize** (min–max): rescale onto $[0, 1]$.
- What changes in the picture(s)?
:::
:::
::: {.column width="62%"}
```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 5.3
#| fig-height: 4.0
#| fig-alt: "The same 90 salaries plotted three times as a row of dots: once on the raw dollar axis, once on a z-score axis running from about −2 to 3, and once on a min–max axis from 0 to 1; the arrangement of the dots is identical in all three, only the axis labels differ"
rng = np.random.default_rng(17)
raw = rng.normal(72_000, 14_000, 90)
FORMS = ["raw salary ($)", "z-score (standardized)", "min–max (normalized)"]
scaled = pl.DataFrame({
    "form": np.repeat(FORMS, len(raw)),
    "v": np.concatenate([raw,
                         (raw - raw.mean()) / raw.std(ddof=1),
                         (raw - raw.min()) / (raw.max() - raw.min())]),
    "y": np.tile(np.zeros(len(raw)), 3)}
).with_columns(pl.col("form").cast(pl.Enum(FORMS)))

(ggplot(scaled, aes("v", "y"))
 + geom_point(color=ORANGE, size=2.5, alpha=0.45)
 + facet_wrap("form", ncol=1, scales="free_x")
 + labs(x="", y="")
 + theme_minimal(base_size=13)
 + theme(strip_text=element_text(size=13, weight="bold", color=INK),
         axis_text_y=element_blank(), panel_grid_major_y=element_blank(),
         panel_grid_minor=element_blank(), figure_size=(5.3, 4.0)))
```
:::
::::

## Basic Functional Relations {.image-frame-slide}

<img src="../assets/viz-basics/functional-relations.svg" alt="Four small plots: y equals x is a straight line; y equals x squared and y equals x cubed curve away from the origin; y equals log x rises steeply then flattens; y equals e to the x is flat then explodes.">


---

## Log: the "Swiss Army Knife" {.text-figure-slide}

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="46%"}
::: {.dense}
A log can turn non-linear relationships into linear ones:

**1. Exponential**

$y = a^{x} \;\Rightarrow\; \log(y) = x \log(a)$

**2. Power law**

$y = a x^{k} \;\Rightarrow\; \log(y) = \log(a) + k \log(x)$

::: {style="font-size:0.85em; margin-top:0.6em;"}
Exponential → log the **y**. Power law → log **both**.
:::
:::
:::
::: {.column width="54%"}
<img class="figure" src="../assets/viz-basics/log-linearize.svg" alt="Two panels of the same exponential curve. On a linear y-axis it is a hockey stick; on a log y-axis it is a straight line.">
:::
:::

# Correlation and Causality {.section-header}

---

## The Correlation Matrix {.figure-aside}

::: {.columns}
::: {.column}
- With $p$ variables there are $\binom{p}{2}$ pairs. A **correlation matrix** puts all of them in one table.
- Symmetric, with 1.00 down the diagonal : so only one triangle carries information.
- Color it on a **diverging** scale: two meaningful ends, a meaningful middle at zero.
- Read it as a *shortlist*, not a result: it tells you which scatter plots to go draw.
:::
::: {.column}

<img class="figure" src="../assets/viz-basics/correlation-matrix.svg" alt="Seven-by-seven correlation matrix of Cook County home sale variables, shaded orange for positive and blue-grey for negative. Building square footage correlates 0.77 with rooms and 0.69 with price; miles from the Loop correlates only minus 0.08 with price.">

::: {.caption}
Data: Cook County single-family sales, 2025.
:::
:::
:::

---

## Reading a Correlation Matrix {.figure-aside}

::: {.columns}
::: {.column}
- Every cell is one number standing in for a whole cloud : the Datasaurus problem, $\binom{p}{2}$ times over.
- A near-zero cell is **not** "no relationship." Price vs. miles from the Loop is $-0.08$ because two effects cancel: far-out homes are bigger and newer, but less central.
- A **scatterplot matrix** costs more ink and keeps the shape.
- Correlation is still not causation : that is the next slide.
:::
::: {.column}

<img class="figure" src="../assets/viz-basics/scatterplot-matrix.svg" alt="Four-by-four scatterplot matrix of price, building square footage, land square footage and year built for 1,400 Cook County sales, with a histogram of each variable on the diagonal. The year-built panels show two distinct clusters that no single correlation reports.">

::: {.caption}
Data: Cook County single-family sales, 2025.
:::
:::
:::

---

## Can we conclude that one causes the other? {.split}

::: {.split-content .golden-columns}

::: {}

<img class="figure" src="../assets/viz-basics/spurious-random-walks.svg" alt="Two series plotted against year on separate left and right y-axes, tracking each other closely, annotated r equals 0.99 and a note that both are random walks from a random number generator with nothing to do with each other." style="max-height:340px;">

**A.** Yes &nbsp;&nbsp; **B.** No

- What does $r = 0.99$ buy you here?
- What would you need in order to say "causes"?
:::

<iframe src="https://dodatascience.fun/timer/" title="CTA-style countdown timer" loading="lazy" style="width: 100%; height: 420px; display: block; border: 1px solid #999; box-shadow: 0 10px 28px rgba(0,0,0,0.12); border-radius: 3px;"></iframe>

:::

---

## Correlation ≠ Causation {.text-figure-slide}

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="46%"}
::: {.dense}
::: {}
- A correlation is consistent with $X \to Y$, with $Y \to X$, with a **common cause** $Z$, and with pure coincidence.
- The **fork** is the classic one: $Z$ causes both, so $X$ and $Y$ move together without touching.
- No amount of extra data points settles which it is. It is not a sample-size problem.
:::
:::
:::
::: {.column width="54%"}
<img class="figure" src="../assets/confounds/fork.svg" alt="Causal diagram with three boxes. A dark box labelled Z sits above two neutral boxes labelled X and Y, with arrows running from Z down to X and from Z down to Y. There is no arrow between X and Y.">
:::
:::

::: {style="font-size:0.78em; margin-top:0.3em;"}
We come back to this properly later in the course. For now, the visualization lesson is that **a chart cannot show you an arrow**.
:::

# Large N, Smoothing & Dimensionality {.section-header}

---

## Nearly 25,000 Points {.image-frame-slide}

<img src="../assets/viz-basics/overplot-solid.svg" alt="Scatter plot of about 24,000 Cook County home sales, building square footage against sale price, with every point drawn fully opaque. The lower left of the plot is a solid black mass with no internal structure.">

::: {style="font-size:0.8em; margin-top:0.4em;"}
Every point is on the page, and the shape of the data is gone. **Overplotting** : the ink saturates and the plot stops being a distribution.
:::

---

## What would be a better plot? {.split}

::: {.split-content .golden-columns}

::: {}

Think about the **type** of data before you answer.

**A.** Histogram / density plot

**B.** Bar plot

**C.** Violin plot

**D.** Box plot

:::

<iframe src="https://dodatascience.fun/timer/" title="CTA-style countdown timer" loading="lazy" style="width: 100%; height: 420px; display: block; border: 1px solid #999; box-shadow: 0 10px 28px rgba(0,0,0,0.12); border-radius: 3px;"></iframe>

:::

---

## Two Fixes for Overplotting {.image-frame-slide}

::: {.r-stack}
<div class="fragment fade-out" data-fragment-index="1"><img src="../assets/viz-basics/overplot-alpha.svg" alt="The same 24,000 sales drawn at 6 percent opacity, so density shows as depth of colour: a bright dense core around 1,200 square feet and 300 thousand dollars fading outward."></div>

<div class="fragment" data-fragment-index="1"><img src="../assets/viz-basics/overplot-hexbin.svg" alt="The same data as a hex-binned two-dimensional histogram with a logarithmic colour scale, showing the same dense core as dark cells and a long sparse fan to the upper right."></div>

:::

::: {style="font-size:0.78em; margin-top:0.3em;"}
**Alpha** lets overlap accumulate into shade. **Hex binning** is the honest version of the same idea: a two-dimensional histogram with a colorbar you can read.
:::

---

## The Conditional Center {.image-frame-slide}

<img src="../assets/viz-basics/overplot-smooth.svg" alt="The faint point cloud of home sales with a thick orange curve running through it, rising steeply from about 250 thousand dollars at 800 square feet to about 1.2 million at 5,000 square feet and flattening at the top.">

::: {style="font-size:0.8em; margin-top:0.4em;"}
A smooth curve of **local averages**: for each $x$, the average $y$ in a neighborhood of $x$. That is the conditional center, and it is what your eye was trying to trace anyway.
:::

---

## Histograms and Bin Width {.text-figure-slide}

::: {.aside-note}
*Learning Data Science*, [Section 11.2: Smoothing and Aggregating Data](https://learningds.org/ch/11/viz_smoothing.html)
:::

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="42%"}
::: {.incremental style="font-size:0.72em; padding-right:20px;"}
- Same 400 heights, three bin counts.
- Too few bins hides shape; too many shows noise.
- Good to try more than one bin width.
- A bin width is a **smoothing choice**, like the bandwidth coming up next.
:::
:::
::: {.column width="58%"}
```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 5.3
#| fig-height: 4.4
#| fig-alt: "The same 400 heights drawn as three stacked histograms with 6, 20 and 60 bins; the 6-bin version is a coarse block, the 20-bin version shows a clean single peak, and the 60-bin version breaks into spiky counts"
rng = np.random.default_rng(9)
h = rng.normal(68, 3.2, 400)
LEVELS = ["6 bins", "20 bins", "60 bins"]

def counted(n, label):
    """One np.histogram per bin count, so a single geom_col draws all three panels."""
    cnt, edges = np.histogram(h, bins=n)
    return pl.DataFrame({"mid": (edges[:-1] + edges[1:]) / 2,
                         "count": cnt.astype(float),
                         "w": np.repeat(edges[1] - edges[0], n),
                         "bins": [label] * n})

bars = pl.concat([counted(n, lab) for n, lab in zip([6, 20, 60], LEVELS)]
                 ).with_columns(pl.col("bins").cast(pl.Enum(LEVELS)))

(ggplot(bars, aes("mid", "count"))
 + geom_col(aes(width="w"), fill=ORANGE, alpha=0.8, color="white", size=0.4)
 + facet_wrap("bins", ncol=1, scales="free_y")
 + labs(x="height (in)", y="count")
 + theme_minimal(base_size=13)
 + theme(strip_text=element_text(size=13, weight="bold", color=INK),
         panel_grid_minor=element_blank(), figure_size=(5.3, 4.4)))
```
:::
::::

---

## Smoothing Detour: Kernel Density {.image-frame-slide}

::: {.r-stack}
<div class="fragment fade-out" data-fragment-index="1"><img src="../assets/viz-basics/kde-1-points.svg" alt="An empty plot with three short tick marks on the x-axis at 2, 3 and 5."></div>

<div class="fragment fade-in-then-out" data-fragment-index="1"><img src="../assets/viz-basics/kde-2-one-kernel.svg" alt="The same three ticks with one grey bell curve centred on the point at 2, annotated that the area under each kernel is one third."></div>

<div class="fragment fade-in-then-out" data-fragment-index="2"><img src="../assets/viz-basics/kde-3-kernels.svg" alt="Three overlapping grey bell curves, one centred on each of the three ticks."></div>

<div class="fragment" data-fragment-index="3"><img src="../assets/viz-basics/kde-4-sum.svg" alt="The three grey bell curves with a thick orange curve above them: their pointwise sum, with a tall peak between 2 and 3 and a second bump at 5."></div>

:::

::: {style="font-size:0.78em; margin-top:0.3em;"}
$\hat{f}(x) = \dfrac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n} K_h(x - x_i)$ : put a kernel on each observation, then add them up. **No bins, no bin edges.**
:::

---

## Bandwidth {.image-frame-slide}

<img src="../assets/viz-basics/kde-bandwidth.svg" alt="Three panels of the same three data points estimated with bandwidths 0.25, 0.75 and 2.0. The narrow bandwidth gives three separate spikes, the middle one gives a two-bump curve, the wide one gives a single broad mound.">

::: {style="font-size:0.8em; margin-top:0.4em;"}
$h$ decides how peaked or spread each kernel is.
:::

---

## Smoothing a Scatter Plot {.image-frame-slide}

::: {.r-stack}
<div class="fragment fade-out" data-fragment-index="1"><img src="../assets/viz-basics/smooth-1-scatter.svg" alt="A scatter plot of about 46 grey points rising from lower left to upper right with noticeable scatter."></div>

<div class="fragment fade-in-then-out" data-fragment-index="1"><img src="../assets/viz-basics/smooth-2-window.svg" alt="The same scatter with a shaded vertical window between x equals 5 and 9; the points inside are orange and a black triangle marks their mean y-value."></div>

<div class="fragment fade-in-then-out" data-fragment-index="2"><img src="../assets/viz-basics/smooth-3-bin-means.svg" alt="The same scatter divided by dashed vertical lines into five bins, with a black triangle at the mean y-value of each bin."></div>

<div class="fragment fade-in-then-out" data-fragment-index="3"><img src="../assets/viz-basics/smooth-4-curve.svg" alt="The bin-mean triangles joined by straight black segments, sketching a rising curve across the point cloud."></div>

<div class="fragment" data-fragment-index="4"><img src="../assets/viz-basics/smooth-5-kernel.svg" alt="The same scatter with a smooth orange curve instead of the jointed segments, produced by kernel weights rather than hard bins."></div>

:::

::: {style="font-size:0.78em; margin-top:0.3em;"}
$g(x) = \sum_i \dfrac{K_h(x - x_i)\,y_i}{\sum_j K_h(x - x_j)}$ : a **weighted average of the $y_i$**, with weights from the kernel. The denominator is there so the weights sum to 1.
:::

---

## Local Smoothing {.text-figure-slide}

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="42%"}
::: {.dense}
::: {}
- A **moving window** over $x$; average (or fit) the $y$ values inside it.
- Many ways to do it: **kernel** methods, cubic and thin-plate **splines**, **lowess**.
- All of them have a bandwidth-shaped knob, and it is always the real decision.
- Reveals the *shape* of the relationship between $y$ and $x$.
:::
:::
:::
::: {.column width="58%"}
<img class="figure" src="../assets/viz-basics/smooth-6-bandwidth.svg" alt="One scatter plot with three kernel-smoothed curves: a wiggly grey curve at bandwidth 0.6, a moderate orange curve at 1.6, and a nearly straight black line at 6.0.">
:::
:::

---

## Smoothing Plus Conditioning {.text-figure-slide}

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="40%"}
::: {.dense}
::: {}
- One smooth curve **per bedroom count**: we have controlled for bedrooms.
- The curves separate, so square footage alone was never the whole story.
- Careful: these are **not longitudinal** (no house was followed as it grew).
- Conditioning removes one alternative explanation. It does not remove the rest.
:::
:::
:::
::: {.column width="60%"}
<img class="figure" src="../assets/viz-basics/smoothing-conditioned.svg" alt="Four smoothed curves of local average sale price against building square footage, one for each of 2, 3, 4 and 5-plus bedrooms. The curves rise together but the 4 and 5-plus curves sit well above the 2 and 3 bedroom curves at the same square footage.">
:::
:::

# matplotlib & ggplot {.section-header}

---

## Recreating the FIFA Chart: Setup

```{python}
#| echo: true
#| output: false
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

sizes  = [63, 27, 10]
labels = ['COL', 'COD', 'In Contest']
colors = ['#f5c800', '#0057a8', '#00a896']

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(4, 4))
```

---

## Recreating the FIFA Chart: Draw {.code-figure-slide}

```{python}
#| echo: true
#| fig-format: svg
#| fig-alt: "Donut chart of FIFA World Cup 2026 Group K possession: Colombia 63% in yellow, DR Congo 27% in blue, In Contest 10% in teal"
ax.pie(sizes, labels=labels, autopct='%1.0f%%',
       colors=colors, startangle=90, counterclock=False,
       wedgeprops=dict(width=0.5), pctdistance=0.75)
ax.set_title('Possession', fontweight='bold')
plt.tight_layout()
```

---

## Recreating the FIFA Chart {.code-figure-slide}

```{python}
#| echo: true
#| fig-alt: "Donut chart of FIFA World Cup 2026 Group K possession: Colombia 63% in yellow, DR Congo 27% in blue, In Contest 10% in teal"
#| fig-format: svg
#| fig-width: 5
#| fig-height: 5
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

sizes  = [63, 27, 10]
labels = ['COL', 'COD', 'In Contest']
colors = ['#f5c800', '#0057a8', '#00a896']
_, ax = plt.subplots()
ax.pie(sizes, labels=labels, autopct='%1.0f%%', colors=colors,
       startangle=90, counterclock=False,
       wedgeprops=dict(width=0.5), pctdistance=0.75)
ax.set_title('Possession', fontweight='bold');
```

## Recreating the FIFA Chart: Polished

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-format: svg
#| fig-alt: "Donut chart styled after the FIFA World Cup 2026 broadcast graphic: Colombia 63% yellow, DR Congo 27% blue, In Contest 10% teal, with legend on the right inside a semi-transparent dark rounded rectangle."
#| out-width: 100%
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import matplotlib.gridspec as gridspec
from matplotlib.patches import FancyBboxPatch

phi = (1 + 5**0.5) / 2  # golden ratio ≈ 1.618
fig_h = 4.5
fig_w = fig_h * phi

fig = plt.figure(figsize=(fig_w, fig_h))
fig.patch.set_alpha(0)

bg = FancyBboxPatch(
    (0.02, 0.03), 0.96, 0.94,
    boxstyle="round,pad=0.03",
    facecolor=(0, 0, 0, 0.72),
    edgecolor="none",
    transform=fig.transFigure,
    zorder=0,
)
fig.add_artist(bg)

gs = gridspec.GridSpec(
    1, 2, width_ratios=[2, 3],
    left=0.03, right=0.97, bottom=0.05, top=0.95, wspace=0,
)
ax_d = fig.add_subplot(gs[0])
ax_l = fig.add_subplot(gs[1])
for ax in (ax_d, ax_l):
    ax.set_facecolor("none")

sizes  = [63, 27, 10]
labels = ["COL", "COD", "IN CONTEST"]
colors = ["#fcd116", "#0057a8", "#00a896"]

# startangle=-90 → Colombia starts at 6 o'clock, counterclock=False → runs clockwise to ~1 o'clock
ax_d.pie(
    sizes, colors=colors, startangle=-90, counterclock=False,
    wedgeprops=dict(width=0.5, edgecolor="white", linewidth=2.5),
)

ax_l.axis("off")
ax_l.set_xlim(0, 1)
ax_l.set_ylim(0, 1)

ax_l.text(0.08, 0.82, "POSSESSION", color="white", fontsize=19,
          fontweight="bold", va="center")

for i, (label, color, pct) in enumerate(zip(labels, colors, sizes)):
    y = 0.60 - i * 0.20
    # white ring behind colored fill
    ax_l.plot(0.10, y, "o", color="white",  markersize=19, zorder=4)
    ax_l.plot(0.10, y, "o", color=color,    markersize=14, zorder=5)
    ax_l.text(0.22, y, label,      color="white", fontsize=16, va="center")
    ax_l.text(0.72, y, f"{pct}%",  color="white", fontsize=16, va="center",
              fontweight="bold");
```

## Recreating the FIFA Chart: R Setup

```{r}
#| echo: true
library(ggplot2)

sizes  <- c(63, 27, 10)
labels <- c("COL", "COD", "In Contest")
colors <- c("#fcd116", "#0057a8", "#00a896")

df <- data.frame(
  label = factor(labels, levels = labels),
  pct   = sizes,
  color = colors
)
```

## Recreating the FIFA Chart: R / ggplot, Bare {.code-figure-slide}

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| dev: svglite
#| fig-alt: "Basic donut chart using ggplot2 coord_polar with default colors: Colombia, DR Congo, In Contest"
ggplot(df, aes(x = 2, y = pct, fill = label)) +
  geom_col(width = 1) +
  coord_polar(theta = "y", start = pi, direction = -1)
```

## Recreating the FIFA Chart: R / ggplot, Colors {.code-figure-slide}

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| dev: svglite
#| code-line-numbers: "4-5"
#| fig-alt: "Donut chart with FIFA colors applied and donut hole created via xlim"
ggplot(df, aes(x = 2, y = pct, fill = label)) +
  geom_col(width = 1) +
  coord_polar(theta = "y", start = pi, direction = -1) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = setNames(df$color, df$label)) +
  xlim(0.5, 2.5)
```

## Recreating the FIFA Chart: R / ggplot, Labels {.code-figure-slide}

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| dev: svglite
#| code-line-numbers: "6-8"
#| fig-alt: "Completed ggplot2 donut chart: Colombia 63% yellow, DR Congo 27% blue, In Contest 10% teal, with Possession title and minimal theme"
ggplot(df, aes(x = 2, y = pct, fill = label)) +
  geom_col(width = 1) +
  coord_polar(theta = "y", start = pi, direction = -1) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = setNames(df$color, df$label)) +
  xlim(0.5, 2.5) +
  labs(title = "Possession", fill = NULL) +
  theme_void() +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", hjust = 0.5))
```

## Recreating the FIFA Chart: R Polished

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| dev: svglite
#| fig-alt: "Polished donut chart styled after FIFA broadcast graphic, made with ggplot2: dark background, Colombia 63% yellow, DR Congo 27% blue, In Contest 10% teal, with colored dot legend"
library(ggplot2)
library(ggtext)
library(patchwork)

sizes  <- c(63, 27, 10)
labels <- c("COL", "COD", "IN CONTEST")
colors <- c("#fcd116", "#0057a8", "#00a896")
df <- data.frame(
  label = factor(labels, levels = labels),
  pct   = sizes,
  color = colors
)

donut <- ggplot(df, aes(x = 2, y = pct, fill = label)) +
  geom_col(width = 1, color = "white", linewidth = 1) +
  coord_polar(theta = "y", start = pi, direction = -1) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = setNames(df$color, df$label)) +
  xlim(0.5, 2.5) +
  theme_void() +
  theme(legend.position = "none",
        plot.background = element_rect(fill = NA, color = NA))

legend_df <- data.frame(
  label = factor(labels, levels = labels),
  pct   = paste0(sizes, "%"),
  color = colors,
  y     = c(0.65, 0.45, 0.25)
)
legend_panel <- ggplot(legend_df, aes(y = y)) +
  annotate("text", x = 0.1, y = 0.85, label = "POSSESSION",
           color = "white", size = 6, fontface = "bold", hjust = 0) +
  geom_point(aes(x = 0.12, color = label), size = 7) +
  geom_text(aes(x = 0.24, label = label), color = "white",
            size = 5, hjust = 0) +
  geom_text(aes(x = 0.95, label = pct), color = "white",
            size = 5, hjust = 1, fontface = "bold") +
  scale_color_manual(values = setNames(df$color, df$label)) +
  xlim(0, 1) + ylim(0, 1) +
  theme_void() +
  theme(legend.position = "none",
        plot.background = element_rect(fill = NA, color = NA))

donut + legend_panel +
  plot_layout(widths = c(2, 3)) &
  theme(plot.background = element_rect(fill = "#000000bb", color = NA))
```

## Comparing matplotlib and ggplot {.smaller}

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}

**Python / matplotlib**

```python
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

sizes  = [63, 27, 10]
labels = ['COL', 'COD', 'In Contest']
colors = ['#fcd116', '#0057a8', '#00a896']

# wedge order + label positions handled by pie()
_, ax = plt.subplots()

ax.pie(sizes, labels=labels, colors=colors,
       autopct='%1.0f%%', pctdistance=0.75,
       startangle=90, counterclock=False,
       wedgeprops=dict(width=0.5))
ax.set_title('Possession', fontweight='bold')
```

:::
::: {.column width="50%"}

**R / ggplot2**

```r
library(ggplot2)

sizes  <- c(63, 27, 10)
labels <- c("COL", "COD", "In Contest")
colors <- c("#fcd116", "#0057a8", "#00a896")

# wedge order + label positions computed by hand
df <- data.frame(label = factor(labels, levels = labels),
                 pct = sizes)
df$pos <- cumsum(df$pct) - df$pct / 2

ggplot(df, aes(x = 2, y = pct, fill = label)) +
  geom_col(width = 1,
           position = position_stack(reverse = TRUE)) +
  geom_text(aes(x = 1.75, y = pos,
                label = paste0(pct, "%"))) +
  geom_text(aes(x = 2.75, y = pos, label = label)) +
  coord_polar(theta = "y", start = 0, direction = 1) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = setNames(colors, labels)) +
  xlim(0.5, 3) +
  labs(title = "Possession") +
  theme_void() +
  theme(legend.position = "none",
        plot.title = element_text(face = "bold",
                                  hjust = 0.5))
```

# Sources {.sources}

1. GitHub source: <https://github.com/jackbandy/data-science-fun/blob/main/docs/slides/week5.qmd>.
2. Pie vs. bar comparison: Schutz, [*Piecharts.svg*](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Piecharts.svg), Wikimedia Commons, 2008. [CC BY 1.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/1.0/).
3. Dimensionality figures redrawn from Solon Barocas, *Understanding Inscrutability*, presented at ["Algorithms and Explanations,"](https://www.law.nyu.edu/centers/ili/events/algorithms-and-explanations) Information Law Institute, NYU School of Law, 27–28 April 2017. Found by way of Meredith Broussard, *More Than a Glitch: Confronting Race, Gender, and Ability Bias in Tech* (MIT Press, 2023; ISBN 9780262047654, paperback 9780262548328), which cites Barocas and Chandler May on visualizing data relationships.
4. 3D pie chart comparison: Cmglee, [*Misleading macworld 3d pie chart.svg*](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Misleading_macworld_3d_pie_chart.svg), Wikimedia Commons. [CC BY-SA 4.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0). Redrawn from the chart shown at Macworld 2008, via [Edward Tufte's notebook on pie charts](https://www.edwardtufte.com/notebook/pie-charts/).
5. Slides developed using materials from [Elena Zheleva](https://www.cs.uic.edu/~elena/) and [Gonzalo Bello Lander](https://cs.uic.edu/profiles/gonzalo-bello/), the Berkeley DS 100 team, Marine Carpuat, and Brian Ziebart.
6. Macworld 2008 keynote clip: ["Macworld San Francisco 2008 Keynote Address (MacBook Air & iTunes Movie Rentals) by Steve Jobs"](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=i9XU6wk_mWY), Apple Keynote Videos (YouTube); market share segment at 8:24–10:10.
7. Visual variables: Jacques Bertin, *Sémiologie graphique: Les diagrammes, les réseaux, les cartes* (Gauthier-Villars, 1967); English translation *Semiology of Graphics: Diagrams, Networks, Maps*, trans. William J. Berg (University of Wisconsin Press, 1983; reissued by Esri Press, 2010).
8. Channels and the effectiveness ranking: Tamara Munzner, *Visualization Analysis & Design* (CRC Press, 2014), ch. 5. Open companion site: <https://www.cs.ubc.ca/~tmm/vadbook/>.
9. Chicago map layers: [chicago-maps](https://github.com/jackbandy/data-science-fun/tree/main/datasets/chicago-maps): city and ward boundaries and ward-level ACS income from the [Chicago Data Portal](https://data.cityofchicago.org/); water polygons from U.S. Census Bureau [TIGERweb](https://tigerweb.geo.census.gov/) areal hydrography.
10. Shape anecdote: Pete Docter on designing characters from basic geometry, in [*Pete Docter | Geometry of Characters*](https://youtu.be/i2tkCBFlXyc?t=398) (Any-mation, 2016), from 6:38. Images in the build: [docs/assets/abstraction](https://github.com/jackbandy/data-science-fun/tree/main/docs/assets/abstraction) : see that folder's `SOURCES.md` for per-image credits.
11. Figures in [docs/assets/viz-basics](https://github.com/jackbandy/data-science-fun/tree/main/docs/assets/viz-basics) are generated by `make_viz_basics_figures.py` from three in-repo datasets : [cook-county-home-sales-2025](https://github.com/jackbandy/data-science-fun/tree/main/datasets/cook-county-home-sales-2025) (Cook County Assessor's Office), [cta-ridership](https://github.com/jackbandy/data-science-fun/tree/main/datasets/cta-ridership) and [chicago-l-stations](https://github.com/jackbandy/data-science-fun/tree/main/datasets/chicago-l-stations) ([Chicago Data Portal](https://data.cityofchicago.org/)) : plus the sources below. See that folder's `SOURCES.md` for the per-figure mapping. CTA route colors follow the [CTA Trademark Guidelines for Developers](https://www.transitchicago.com/developers/branding/).
12. Scale example: the chart Rep. Jason Chaffetz displayed at the House Committee on Oversight and Government Reform hearing, 29 September 2015, reproducing a figure from an [Americans United for Life](https://aul.org/) report. Service counts are Planned Parenthood's own published annual figures for 2006 and 2013.
13. Color: Masataka Okabe and Kei Ito, ["Color Universal Design"](https://jfly.uni-koeln.de/color/) (2008); Françoise Viénot, Hans Brettel and John D. Mollon, "Digital video colourbars for testing dichromatic colour vision," *Color Research & Application* 24, no. 4 (1999): 243–252; Nathaniel Smith and Stéfan van der Walt, ["A Better Default Colormap for Matplotlib"](https://bids.github.io/colormap/) (SciPy 2015).
14. Smoothing and the Cherry Blossom run analysis the Large-N section is modeled on: Deborah Nolan and Duncan Temple Lang, *Data Science in R: A Case Studies Approach to Computational Reasoning and Problem Solving* (CRC Press, 2015), ch. 2.
15. Slide deck built with [Quarto](https://quarto.org/) revealjs. Title font is Big Shoulders; body font is [Libre Franklin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Franklin_Gothic#Libre_Franklin).
16. Simpson's paradox figures are generated from synthetic data; the two-panel layout is modeled on Gordon Goodwin, ["Simpson's Paradox: One Chart, Two Realities"](https://www.linkedin.com/pulse/simpsons-paradox-one-chart-two-realities-gordon-goodwin-hhhte).
17. Line graphs, the area principle, and the density scale: Ani Adhikari, John DeNero and David Wagner, *Computational and Inferential Thinking: The Foundations of Data Science*, [ch. 7](https://inferentialthinking.com/chapters/07/visualization) and [§7.2](https://inferentialthinking.com/chapters/07/2/visualizing-numerical-distributions). The area principle example there is from [Flowing Data](https://flowingdata.com/).
18. Geospatial idioms and uncertainty: Claus O. Wilke, *Fundamentals of Data Visualization* (O'Reilly, 2019), [ch. 5](https://clauswilke.com/dataviz/directory-of-visualizations.html) and [ch. 16](https://clauswilke.com/dataviz/visualizing-uncertainty.html).
19. The principle of proportional ink: Carl Bergstrom and Jevin West, *Calling Bullshit*, [7.3](https://www.callingbullshit.org/tools/tools_proportional_ink.html); the phrase is Bergstrom's restatement of Tufte's lie factor.
20. Batting averages: Ken Ross, *A Mathematician at the Ballpark: Odds and Probabilities for Baseball Fans* (Pi Press, 2004); Derek Jeter's and David Justice's 1995 and 1996 lines are as published by [Baseball Reference](https://www.baseball-reference.com/).
21. Donut version of the Macworld chart: drawn by `make_macworld_donut.py` in [docs/assets/pi-donut-demos](https://github.com/jackbandy/data-science-fun/tree/main/docs/assets/pi-donut-demos), from the market share figures (Gartner, CQ3 2007) printed on the keynote slide; wedge order and colors match the flat pie panel above.
